utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case for today.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances for today, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Dan Saxon for the Prosecution with my colleagues Salvatore Cannata, Carolyn Edgerton, and Carmela Javier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. On behalf of the Defence, today in the courtroom there is me, Novak Lukic, Gregor Guy-Smith, and our case manager Danijela Tasic, and our assistant, Milos Androvic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honours, Ms. Edgerton will call the witness this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton, are there any special arrangements for this witness, or is she an ordinary witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: This witness has protected measures from the last proceeding she testified in, Your Honours. As per a notification the Prosecution filed, she has facial distortion, and of course those measures apply, and we'd ask that that be made the case for her testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want us then to go into closed session before she walks in?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think that would be appropriate, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have anybody in the gallery? You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do you recall coming to testify in February 2007 before another Trial Chamber of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, to prepare for your testimony today, did my colleagues read back to you the questions asked and the answers you gave during that previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Was that in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you understand everything that you heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Did you also have a chance to look at the copies of photographs and documents and maps you referred to during that testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And did that also include a copy of a statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor for this Tribunal in 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, if I asked you all the same questions today in respect of that evidence, would you give the same answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That being the case, Your Honours, may I move into evidence, and I'll refer to the 65 ter numbers, the previous testimony associated exhibits and statement of this witness from the Dragomir Milosevic proceedings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are the 65 ter numbers?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: For the previous testimony, the 65 ter number is 09305; the associated exhibits are 09301, 02, and 03, all of which are colour photographs; 09304, which is a map; and 05791, which is a document; and finally, the ICTY statement from 23 February 1996, which is 09300.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. All those documents are admitted into evidence. May they please be given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 09305 will be Exhibit P115, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 09301 will be Exhibit P116; 09302 will be Exhibit P117; 09303 will be Exhibit P118; 09304 will be Exhibit P119; 05791 will be Exhibit P120; and finally, 09300 will be Exhibit P121, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, with your leave, I'll just read a brief summary, and then I have a couple of clarifying questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. This witness has been a resident of the area of Dobrinja since 1985 and was injured in the shelling of the Simon Bolivar school on June 18, 1995. By that date residents of Dobrinja had been without water or electricity for about a month. Water pumps were improvised throughout the area. Water was rationed when it was available. The witness's husband often went out at night to collect water because of sniper activity during the day. On the morning of 18 June 1995, the witness queued for water from a pump located in an open area in the ruin of the Simon Bolivar school, which had been destroyed by a fire from a shelling earlier in the war. In order to reach the school, the witness had to cross a playground which was generally unsafe due to sniping, which the witness believes originated from the nearby Nedzarici neighbourhood controlled by the Bosnian Serb army. The witness was one of the first people in line for water. There were approximately 50 to 70 people behind her. She was standing in a door frame when the shell struck. Mrs. Sisic was injured in the heel and upper area of her right leg. A total of seven people were killed as a result of the impact, including two of her neighbours, while 11 or 12 people were injured. And that concludes the summary, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just as I'd indicated, a couple of clarifying questions, the first actually relating to a map which appears in everyone's map book as map number 8. And because the copy which is uploaded in e-court is in black and white, I've had a colour copy identical to the one prepared in your map books produced because I think it's much easier for the witness to see. Could I ask that this be shown to the witness, please. Yes, we will need it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Ma'am, do you recognise generally what the map on the machine beside you depicts? Do you know what that's a map of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the map of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, just so that we can all orient ourselves, are you generally able to indicate with a circle the area of the old town of Sarajevo, or the city centre, let's say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean one circle around both the centre and the old town?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My apologies, and I'll be clear. Let's say the old town first.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you put a number 1 inside that circle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the city centre that I'd mentioned previously, could you roughly indicate the general area of the city centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And you've drawn another circle around that. Could you put a 2 inside that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you generally indicate the area of Dobrinja settlement, where you lived, also with another circle.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And could you put a 3 inside that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, could you perhaps, having lived in Dobrinja for so long, give us an indication how far the distance one would have had to travel by road would be to get from Dobrinja to the old town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's about 10 to 15 kilometres' distance. In terms of time, it would be 10, 15 minutes by car, or 15 to 20 minutes by car.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, in order to travel by car, let's say, what's the most direct route? Could you draw a line indicating the road you might take normally to go from Dobrinja to Sarajevo city centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Everything is so small on this map, it's rather difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is there a map of which that kind of detail can be shown, Madam Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Had we done the e-court absolutely correctly, we would have been able to zoom in. So what I think I'll do is leave this now and ask that it be marked as an exhibit and go to an electronic cut-out that I have of the map where the witness can see more detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With that being said, could this paper copy of the map be tendered, please, as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The map is tendered into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P122, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, and this might take a couple of seconds to call up in e-court, could I ask for the cut-out of map 02719, and in fact, Your Honour, it is a cut-out, as I've just said, of the map we've just seen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'm told it's on e-court as some kind of an attachment to the larger document, Madam Registrar. You've seen it? Thank you. I'm sorry, that's the original document. I'm looking for the cut-out of the larger document that's there as an attachment. I think Mrs. Javier is going to re-release them. My apologies, Your Honour. Great. There we have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Mrs. Sisic, do you see on the screen in front of you a map that has some more detail than the one you previously looked at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You can see more of this part of town where Dobrinja is, but I don't see the centre, and I don't see the old town. In fact, I don't see the old town.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's quite okay. I'm going to ask you a couple of questions based on this map. Are you able to indicate on this map the approximate location of where you lived on the 18th of June, 1995? And you'll remember from your previous testimony, you'll need to do that with the pen my colleague will hand you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I put a circle around it?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A small one, please, and you can mark it with the number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I crossed the school ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So you've marked the Simon Bolivar school, I take it, or your apartment building? I'm not sure I understood.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My building where I lived, I touched upon the school but the school is not within the circle.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right. So I take it from what you've said that the school is immediately proximate to your building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, are you able to indicate with an arrow what the main road would be connecting Dobrinja to the city centre, if you were going to travel by car?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know how to do that. Maybe this road here. It's kind of difficult, but I'll try. It's this road. Is this okay?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So the point of the arrow is, as I understand you, leaving from Dobrinja towards the city centre.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, I made a mistake. If you allow me, this road was used only very little. What we did is went through the settlement. I can't see the road clearly because I'm --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- we used a shortcut.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Madam Witness, I'd like to know - my question was and I'll try and explain it a little more clearly - I'd like to know if you can mark the main road that you would have used before the war to travel by car from Dobrinja to the Sarajevo city centre. And perhaps we could, since you've indicated we made a mistake, erase the line that you've made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How does she erase it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the main road.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If she shifts the map, she can erase it, but she will erase also the circle around her house.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I always understand that my colleague should be able to take it away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Oh, okay. That's -- we learn all the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a good day when that happens to each of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat my question, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understood your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had just made an arrow, and it is indeed the road that we used before the war, and of course we use it today, but it was little used during the war. We went in between buildings, across parking lots --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am, the question was: Mark the road that you used before the war. That was the question. Mark that road.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, the marking that you placed on the map that looks like an upside-down V is the main traffic road you used before the war and today based on what you said to get from Dobrinja to the city centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, keeping this map on the screen, I have a couple of questions related to your previous testimony. At pages 2832 and 2862 of the transcript of your previous testimony, you referred to the area of Nedzarici as being the source of sniper fire which would hit the playground area in front of your apartment. Now, are you able to see and mark with a circle the general area of Nedzarici on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Could you put a 2 inside that circle, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at both of those same pages of your previous testimony you said that Nedzarici was, as far as you knew, being held by the Bosnian Serb army. How do you know that? What's the basis for that statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shots came from that area, from that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So that actually seems to answer a question which I haven't put that says -- that would be: How do you know the origin of fire? But my question -- and thank you for that. My question is: How do you know that, as you said, it was the Serb army that held that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were surrounded. We were not able to move very far. We could only move around Dobrinja, and even that was life-threatening. It was at each of our's own risk.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I'm not quite clear, ma'am. The interpretation said you are saying you were surrounded. Are you saying the whole area of Dobrinja was surrounded by Serbs, Serb armies, or are you saying the Serb army was in Nedzarici only, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that both Dobrinja and Sarajevo as a whole were surrounded by the Serb troops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, ma'am. But the lawyer is trying to find out more about the source of the fire that injured you on the day in question or that was attacking the area of Dobrinja during that time. She's not asking about the whole of Sarajevo; she's asking about Dobrinja only. Now, I want to know: Are you saying that Dobrinja was surrounded, or are you saying that there were soldiers stationed in Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dobrinja was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just related to that, one more question, perhaps to try to get closer to the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: How do you know it was the Serb army in Nedzarici and not the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? How do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the fire came from that direction, and we were not able to move towards that direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: All right, thank you. I'll move on to another question related to your previous testimony. At page 2836 you seem to have tried to illustrate to the Trial Chamber the distance between you and the water pump when the explosion occurred, and the measure didn't quite come across because you said, It's about as far as the distance between me and the door, and I wonder if you can give us an estimate, perhaps in metres, as to how far you were when the explosion occurred.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Some 10 metres away from the pump. That was the distance between me and the pump.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I have one last question, and we'll just keep this map up on the screen for a moment, please. At page 2840 you said that Dobrinja was regularly shelled and all Sarajevo was shelled as well. And my question about that is: How do you know that, that Sarajevo was shelled as well, if you were in Dobrinja some kilometres from the city centre? What's the basis for your assertion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a sister living downtown and some relatives of mine as well. When Dobrinja was blocked across Nedzarici, it was very dangerous to pass through that area, and I was bound for work. Of course, it was up to me to decide whether I would want to show up for work or not because of the danger. My company was housed in the old town, and it was my decision to go to work nevertheless. The danger it involved was grave, but fortunately nothing happened to me. There were shots fired. The targets were even the public transportation means.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So I understand from what you're saying that you know the situation in the whole city during the conflict because you did travel to work from Dobrinja to the city centre and back again when you could.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this is a leading question, after all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for a moment. I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: So based on what you're saying, did you receive information as to the situation in the whole of the city from your sister and your relatives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But of course, and I was myself witness to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: What did you hear, first, from your sister and your relatives, and then tell us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not been objecting to this line of questioning so far because the emphasis was, and I was able to see this from the statements and the testimony, on what was contained in the summary; however, now a completely new topic is being broached, one that I did not expect would be raised in view of what the Prosecutor has indicated to us. We are coming to a new area now that was not notified to us in the proofing note, and that's the area of incidents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect, Your Honour, the indication was that the witness was going to explain -- the indication in the proofing note was that the witness was going to explain the basis for her assertion that all of Sarajevo was shelled, as well as Dobrinja, and my question -- my original question was, What's the basis for your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The problem with the Bench is that that very issue is not mentioned anywhere in her statement. Her statement doesn't talk about her knowledge of shelling in Sarajevo. She talks about how she got injured on the 18th of June, if you look at her statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: My question was with respect to the line in her previous testimony as opposed to her statement, Your Honour, line 2840, and it was to clarify the basis of that assertion -- please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just another point while you're referring to line 2840 --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Sorry, page 2840.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You keep referring us to these pages without giving us the lines, and it takes us time to find what you're referring to. Please, can you, when you make a reference, give us the line as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. Shall I do that now for 2840?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do that for 2840 and remember to do that in the future.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course, and my apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: The line references for the passage that I was seeking to clarify, Your Honour, is 2840, lines 16 to 20, and in particular line 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Still, Your Honour, I have to object. I did not give -- get an indication of this in the proofing note, and I believe that the Prosecutor ought to have indicated it in the proofing note. If the Prosecutor wanted to clarify this sentence concerning the shelling of Sarajevo, she should have informed me of what she would be dealing with on the basis of what the witness had told her. I don't have that sort of notification from the proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've asked you to ...

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, note 5 of the proofing note bears the wrong page number of the transcript. Note 5 says: "Referring to page 2836 of her previous testimony, the witness will explain the basis for her assertion that the whole of Sarajevo was shelled." Your Honour, I've made another mistake with respect to referring to the page numbers, and that didn't assist my friend or the Chamber in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We don't have your proofing notes, ma'am, and so we have no assistance at all in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No. And I am just saying mea culpa --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I understand something here? This is something that's springing on me for the first time. Must the Defence be notified of every little point that is going to be raised in the proofing note or must the Defence be given a copy of the testimony of the witness in the previous case and a copy of the statement and the proofing note, to the extent that it summarises whatever proofing was done, and is the indication not that therefore anything that is in those documents can be touched upon? I need guidance here. In other words, I'm trying to understand your objection, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the gist of my objection is that if this is a witness testifying under 92 ter, or viva voce, and if the Prosecutor learns of a new incident or a new event that the Prosecutor wishes to raise, we have to be informed of the contents of the incident, of the substance of the incident. Above all, I believe that we should not only be informed of that but also be informed in advance. If the topic of the Prosecutor is the general situation in Sarajevo and if the witness now wishes to explain that the situation was such and such for these reasons, then I have to be aware of this in advance in order to prepare myself for that, rather than being surprised by the topic in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Precisely, Mr. Lukic. My question is for you to get this advanced notice, must that be made, that notice be made in the proofing note, or is it sufficient that that point is referred to in any of the documents that you have received, and any of those documents could be, indeed, the proofing note, could be the statement of the witness, could be the testimony of the witness in a previous case? And I'm saying -- I'm asking the question: If the Prosecutor touches on a point that is in any one of these documents but the proofing note, are you saying she's not entitled to do that? Is that the basis for your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may consult with my colleague, Mr. Guy-Smith. We have already discussed the matter, and it is an important issue for the future.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our position is the following, Your Honour: If the Prosecutor wants to, in the course of the examination of the witness, touch upon a qualification of a matter that was -- that concerned the witness and if this matter has not been specifically mentioned in the earlier documents but if the issue appears as a completely novel issue in the proofing note, then the Prosecutor must give us a detailed description of the incident. If the issue concerns a matter that was dealt with specifically in the earlier statements or testimonies and if, on that basis, we are able to prepare for the cross-examination, this issue need not be described in the proofing note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm trying to read the translation of what you've just said because I'm not understanding what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Shall I stop and listen? Okay, you tell me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, only because proofing notes, and I have a kind of a long history. Essentially, we understand the function of a proofing note to be where the Prosecution has obtained information which is distinct from, different to, or contradictory of information that previously existed either in the form of testimony or a statement. When such a condition arises, the Prosecution is to inform the Defence so that we have specific information with regard to either a contradiction or actual shift in the witness's testimony --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- or an expansion of the witness's testimony which could be considered to be distinct. And the difficulty that we have in this particular case is that -- and I'm not being, for the moment, critical yet because I think there's a distinction in terms of the views that we have about what we call "incidents," and I put that in quotes. When a witness now begins to testify about additional incidents which have not been scheduled or otherwise mentioned beforehand, information which we were not privy to before, it's our understanding that this information is information that should be contained in the proofing notes because it now raises a distinct evidential factual matter, potentially a distinct evidential conceptual matter that we beforehand had not been privy to. I hope that's of some assistance in terms of what our thinking and understanding is, because what the whole idea here is, is that the Prosecution, by virtue of the proofing procedure, however you wish to define that procedure, has obtained new information which actually constitutes another statement, and that new information is information which we're entitled to in terms of preparing and properly cross-examining a witness. This is the reason why I said beforehand that it would be a good idea to have verbatim copies of proofing notes in case we ever got involved in any disputes about what was going on. Once again, here's another example where what you have is an expansion of previous testimony, so it's new information. It's a new statement that we don't have. And it's coupled --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is new, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What's new -- what's new at this point, and I may be taking some liberty with my colleague's -- with my colleague's analysis of this particular factual situation, but what's new, as I understand it, is that the basis of an opinion which is now based upon factual material, as the witness has testified, she received information from certain specific places, is new information for us. This is information we did not have before, information could be coming from -- it could be coming from a sourced place, it could be coming from an unsourced place, it could be coming from a sourced place that occurred after many years. I mean, there are a variety of ways that this could come to the witness, and I mean no disrespect whatsoever to the witness. But rather, the fact of the matter is -- the fact of the matter is with regard to the information itself, if we don't know what that information is, then we are not in a position to figure out how to deal with it. And I hope I'm being clear, but I see that you still have a question about what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just ask this one thing. See, the information that I thought we were talking about is the assertion by the witness of the attack of the whole of Sarajevo, and I'm not quite sure whether this is new information or this is information that is already contained in the statement of the witness. Your colleague says, she referenced it as 2836, she meant to say 2840, lines 16 to 20, and what I do find to be new in her line of questioning is when she wants to know how the witness knew that, but not the attack itself. The attack it already -- it's old news.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We're on the exact same page, Your Honour. We're on the exact same page. And our submission is this, and I hazard a guess here in terms of what happened during the proofing session: During the proofing session, either Ms. Edgerton or one of her colleagues said, Listen, you testified to this particular matter, referring to the proper page. She said, Yes, I did. They said, Well, how did you get that information? What is that testimony based on? And the witness said at that point said, This testimony is based upon the following information, not the -- as you've put it, not the issue of the attack itself, but this is how I came to that conclusion. That's information that we don't have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that's what is being objected to.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just your indulgence for a moment, Your Honour, while I consult with my colleague, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: After having spoken with my colleagues and reviewed my friend's position, and taking into consideration the time we're spending on a matter like this -- actually, can I digress for a moment, Your Honour, before I risk losing it and we move much further. Could I ask that the marked map be admitted as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The marked map is admitted as an exhibit. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P123, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Taking into consideration everything, including the amount of time we're spending on this kind of issue with this kind of witness, Your Honour, I think this is as far as I will go with the witness, and I will withdraw the question that my friend is objecting to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And when you say "this is as far as you will go with the witness," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I mean that my examination of the witness is concluded now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now that you have concluded your examination-in-chief, can I raise a concern now that I have?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I am taking into account the fact that this objection took long, but for a person who's coming here on a 92 ter basis, I think we've been very long with this witness, and I've been finding the leading of witnesses, 92 ter witnesses, to be rather too long and wondering why don't you just call them viva voce, because of the time that we take with them. It's just a concern that I'm putting on the table. I would like the Prosecution to please take care of it because you are the people who are calling the witnesses at this point in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Understood, Your Honour, and we'll take it into account and discuss it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, good morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Novak Lukic, and I will be putting some questions to you on behalf of the Defence team for Mr. Perisic. Throughout the war you lived in Dobrinja, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have a question for you arising from your discussions with the Prosecution. You said until the time when Nedzarici was liberated, do you recall when it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nedzarici was not liberated, and I can't give you a date because I'm not a military expert and I did not move about a great deal. However, the road that we could use was liberated, although one could use it at one's own risk. There were trenches that were dug out for pedestrians to use, although you could use a vehicle, but it was shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You didn't say what time period that was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was sometime in 1993 or 1994 that the trenches were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dobrinja is a residential area, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was the entire neighbourhood of Dobrinja under the control of the BH army, and you'll know what I mean by "under the control," or were parts of the Dobrinja area under the control of the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose that your question has to do with whether I could move about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, my question was simple. Was the entire area of Dobrinja --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the centre of Dobrinja was an area where one could move about freely. Is that sufficient an answer? Of course one could move about at one's own risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We will have to slow down, both of us. Can you please make a pause before answering my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were parts of the Dobrinja area specifically named to the effect that you had Dobrinja 1, 2, 3, and 4?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that the separation line, and when I say "the separation line," I'm referring to the line dividing the BH army on the one hand and the Serbian army on the other, was some 400 to 500 metres away from the Simon Bolivar school where the incident took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the distance may have been a bit greater than the one you indicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that some 200 metres away from the school there was the command post of the 155th Mountain Brigade of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The numbers mean -- do not mean anything to me, and I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, were you generally aware of the existence of a command post of a unit of the BH army nearby?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Within the neighbourhood of Dobrinja itself, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Ismet Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber who he is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His role was something that I couldn't tell you really, precisely. He was responsible for --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll tell you. Commander of the 155th Brigade of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And it was his command post that was located there that you said you knew about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time or later on, did you hear that on the 15th of June, so several days before the incident, a large offensive was launched by the BH army on the Sarajevo front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You don't know at all that there was an offensive taking place at the time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'll ask you some matters concerning your statement and testimony. You said - and that's at page 2844, line 4, Your Honours - that the water pump was the safest in Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was the safest pump because it was within an enclosure. It was within the compound of the school that had been shelled at the start of the war and only a skeleton of it remained, whereas all the other water pumps were out in the open, although I didn't go there to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Although you didn't go there, you said. I believe your husband did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That pump had never been shelled before that incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think so, no, save for the fact that the school itself was targeted at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the shell had fallen, you said - and it's transcript page 2656, line 10 - that you did not see anything at that moment, that you were in a daze, and you managed to crawl away. So may I conclude that you did not see who stayed in that area and what happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course, not until I came around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, Mr. Lukic, and I know the witness has answered it. You said: "So may I conclude that you did not see who stayed in that area and what happened next?" What do you mean by "stayed"? Who remained there after the explosion? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness and I understood each other. Perhaps there is a slight error in the interpretation. What I meant is, on the spot where the shell fell, she did not see anything happening in that spot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness marked a map a moment ago, I hope I can have the assistance of the court officer. It's map 02, 2719. I would like to have that same map unmarked, an unmarked copy of the coloured map, 65 ter 2719, because I can see the witness finds it easier to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you see the Sarajevo airport on this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now you will take the pen you have next to you, and on the screen itself would you please circle the central area of the airport and mark it with a 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is this all right? Can you erase this so I can try again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time who controlled the airport?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was injured?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you see Butmir in this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you place number 2 there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you agree with me that Butmir was controlled by BH forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see Alipasino Polje in this map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I suppose it is here, these buildings here.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you mark it with 3. In fact, it's even written Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who controlled that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see Mojmilo area and the Mojmilo hill?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can see the writing -- yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you place a 4 there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was also controlled by the BH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you see Donji Kotorac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mark it with 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who controlled that area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe it's also the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I tender this map into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This map is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D4, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Any re-examination, Madam Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Just one small thing, Your Honour, if I can go back up to the -- to page 26, line 20.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Madam, my friend said to you at page 26, line 20: "After the shell had fallen," and he referred to a page of your previous testimony 28 -- it's written in here 2656, but I'm sure he meant 2856, line 10, and he said to you: "After the shell had fallen, you said that you didn't see anything at that moment, that you were in a daze and you managed to crawl away. So I may conclude that you did not see who stayed in that area and what happened next." And your answer was: "Of course, not until I came around." Now, do you remember my colleagues and I read back to you your previous testimony from the Dragomir Milosevic case? Do you remember that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Now, at page 2856, lines 9 and 10, you said: "My eyes went --" in respect of the impact of the shell. "My eyes went blind at that moment, so I didn't see those people. When I was rising to my feet, I did see people around me." Do you remember giving that answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And do you stand by that answer today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's approximately what I said to the gentleman, that when I came around, only then did I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Edgerton. Judge? Judge, questions for the witness? Thank you, ma'am. This brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to testify. You are now excused, and you may stand down. Please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Edgerton? Mr. Saxon?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: A concern that we should have gone into private session for her leaving, Your Honour. She has facial distortion, if you'll recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm so sorry. How do we rectify that situation at this stage?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm told the cameras were away. But supposing they were not away, how do we -- is there any way we can correct the situation at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I think Your Honour can, for the broadcast outside of the Tribunal, now order a redaction of that portion of the tape, so that will be taken from the external broadcast.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Fine. It's ordered, then, that we will redact the walking out of the witness from court.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And I'm not sure anymore what the delay is for the internal broadcast. It may be too late, but we may have 15 minutes. I just simply don't recall at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Whatever may have happened, we ask that that part be redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm being told there's just nothing to redact because her face was not shown at that time. But I did think that even if there's nothing to redact, you can have a blank -- a dark colour on that part, just to show that you meant to do that. You don't redact only when there's writing or something. But I don't know this technology so --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I don't either, but thank you for the extra precautions you've indicated you wish to take, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done, Madam Edgerton?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'll take my leave now, Your Honour, if we could just have a moment to switch chairs, to return sometime later on this morning. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see Mr. Saxon is standing. Mr. Saxon, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Cannata will lead the next witness, but I do see the time, and perhaps it would make sense now to take the first break before the next witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So we don't repeat what happened yesterday. Let's take the break now and come back at a quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon. Oh, is it Mr. Cannata? Sorry, Mr. Cannata. Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: The Prosecution calls Witness Andja Gotovac. Your Honours, this is a 92 ter witness, for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And there's no protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, ma'am. You may be seated. Yes, Mr. Cannata.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Good morning, madam. How are you today?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can you please state your full name, place and date of birth, for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Andja Gotovac. The 23rd of March, 1930. Travnik, Vucja Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you give two statements to the Office of the Prosecutor on 12th March 1997 and 17 May 2006?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Can I have 65 ter 9278 on the e-court, please. Thank you. Can I have it zoomed in at the -- where the signature is at the bottom on the right. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you see a document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you see your signature on the English document?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Was this document read out to you in a language you understand yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you confirm that what you say in the document -- in the statement is true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Would you say the same if you were asked to speak about the same events today?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I move 65 ter 9278 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P124, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I have now 65 ter 9279 on the e-court, please. Can I have it zoomed down to the signature part -- okay, that's good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you see a document in front of you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Do you see your signature on the document --

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Yes. Was this document read out to you yesterday in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And do you confirm today that what you say in the statement is true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge and belief?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Would you say the same statement if you were asked to speak about the same events today? Would you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. I may have forgotten some bits in the meantime, but most of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this document into evidence? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P125, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Madam Witness, do you -- did you testify in -- before this Tribunal in the case, Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic, last year?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Was a copy of your testimony in this case read out to you in a language you understand yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Did you also have an opportunity to review a copy of the medical record attached to that transcript?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Now, do you confirm that what you said in your testimony in the case, Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic, is true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: It is true, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Would you give the same answers today if asked the same questions?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would like to tender into evidence 65 ter 9280, which is the transcript from the Dragomir Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 9280 is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P126, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: And also 65 ter 4487, which is the exhibit associated to the transcript, and I would like to tender this exhibit under seal, and I can give you the reasons for that. First of all, it's because this document was admitted under seal in previous proceedings, namely, Prosecutor versus Dragomir Milosevic. Secondly, it's a medical record about the witness and putting this -- putting the exhibit under seal will protect the witness's privacy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Cannata. 65 ter 4487 is admitted into evidence under seal. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P127, under seal, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. At this point I would like to read a short summary of the witness's evidence, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have the leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Witness Andja Gotovac has given evidence in respect of scheduled incident A5 of the indictment, that is, the incident that occurred on 24 May 1995 in Safeta Zajke Street in Sarajevo, when two civilians were killed and at least five, including the witness Gotovac herself, were wounded by the explosion of a projectile. The witness testified at on 24 May 1995, at around 10 a.m., she was sitting outside her house in Safeta Zajke Street when she was hit by the explosion of a projectile. As a result of such explosion, Witness Gotovac sustained serious injuries. The witness testified that she never saw any Bosnian army soldiers or positions in the vicinity of the area where she -- where the explosion which resulted in her wounding occurred. Your Honour, that completes my examination-in-chief. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Gotovac, good morning.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My name is Novak Lukic. I'm the lawyer who will be putting questions to you now on behalf of the Defence for Mr. Perisic. Mr. Prosecutor has just briefly reminded the Trial Chamber of your previous statements and testimonies. In my understanding, you gave two statements to the OTP, and you testified in the Milosevic case. On one occasion you gave to the OTP a short statement that you had given to the police.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me leave out the proofing for the earlier testimony and the one you had yesterday. Had you had any other interviews with the Bosnian authorities concerning this incident?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You're a pensioner, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You used to work in a factory, did you not? Can you repeat your answer audibly?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please pause for a second after my question so that the interpretation can run. Can you tell me what it was that you did in the factory.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: I worked in the textile factory called Sik.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That was in Sarajevo, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you worked there as a textile worker, I presume?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did anybody from your family or from your immediate environment have anything to do with the army? Was anybody an active member of the army, an officer, or perhaps one of your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Well, how should I know who was a member of the army? None of my family were, since we were mostly women anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your first statement, that's Exhibit P124, in paragraph 2, you said that you were hit by a modified air bomb. That's what the statement says. Can you tell me what is a modified air bomb, or aerial bomb?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. I was in the front yard when I heard the sound of a plane. There was an explosion and it was -- it was a tube, a barrel, on the ground. That's what they talked about and that's what I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can therefore conclude that it was from the stories that you heard that what hit the ground was a modified aerial bomb.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Well, I know what a bomb is, but this was a long barrel, and I saw it. I went past it in my yard as they were taking me to the hospital when I was wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what an aerial bomb looks like?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness please repeat her answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness has been requested to repeat her answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- speak audibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ma'am, could you speak audibly. May I ask that the microphones be brought a little closer to the witness. I'm mindful of the injuries of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You have to speak up a bit. Relax, Madam Gotovac. My question was: Do you know what an aerial bomb looks like?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony, at page 4463, line 12, and in your statement, the first statement you gave, in paragraph 4, you said that you had heard stories about the bomb having come from Trebevic, according to some, or from Hresa, according to others.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. I don't know about that. It was something others were talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may interrupt. Mr. Cannata, my copy of the witness's transcript does not have pages 4456 to 4464.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: The reason being because the Prosecution didn't tender that part of the transcript. The Prosecution only tendered the examination-in-chief of Ms. Gotovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But now Mr. Lukic is asking the witness about something that's on page 4463, which we don't have.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: I can provide you with a hard copy of these transcripts, if that might assist the Chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. I thought the purpose was that we can follow, so if we don't have the pages right --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Your Honour, read out the relevant part to make it easier and to have that portion in the transcript. The page is 4463, line 2. [In English] "I don't know myself from which direction the projectile came, but I was told that it came from Hresa." Line 12: Some people say it came from Hresa, and other people say from Trebevic. I don't know where it came from. I'm not sure where it came from."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I saw that the Prosecutor was on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just wanted to put in the record that it was not part of the Prosecution obligation to upload on the e-court portions of the transcripts which the Prosecution didn't seek leave to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Madam Gotovac, did you perhaps hear stories about the distance that the bomb may have covered?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: No, I didn't, because at that point all of us, the dead and the wounded, were taken to the hospital, and later on I didn't hear any such stories. In fact, I was avoiding it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My question implied whether you had heard such stories later on, not at that time. But you have given me your answer. Your first statement given to the OTP - that's Exhibit 114, paragraph 3 - says something you said just now, that you heard a sound which reminded you of the sound of a plane. You looked up to see who it was, the madman who flew so low, and then you heard the explosion. Can you tell me: How much time has elapsed between the time you heard the noise of the plane and the explosion itself?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: A couple of seconds, I guess. There was mayhem right away. It was horrific. At that point I wasn't able to know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you heard the sound that at first was quite soft and then became louder.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that's when you -- when that thought crossed your mind.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In your testimony, at page -- rather, paragraph 3 of the same statement, you said that your quarter of town was shelled. Were you able to distinguish between the sounds of mortars, howitzers, tank shells? Were you able to do that at the time?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: No. It was quite difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also testified at page 4458, line 5, and in the second statement, paragraph 3, you said that there were no snipers active in your neighbourhood and that you could freely move about the area.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: That's correct. There were none.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that sniper incidents only took place close to the front line?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: They happened throughout the town. But since we're a bit away, we're on the edge of town, we didn't have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about your second statement, paragraph 3. You said: "Our part of town was sufficiently removed from the front lines, and we did not have to worry about snipers." This is what you said.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, our quarter of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And that's how I concluded that snipers were active in the proximity of the front lines.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know how I should explain this to you now. If you take the main streets, the Titova Street, Grbavica, up there, there were snipers, including Hrasno.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And the Miljacka separated the warring parties, did it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the BH army had snipers, mortars, howitzers?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor has just referred to paragraph 4 of your second statement where you said that there had never been any army in your neighbourhood. You said that, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the army passed through your neighbourhood on their way to Zuc mount where the BH army had positions?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: They probably did pass through the area, but since I spent most of the time in shelter, more time in shelter than I did in my home or in the street - I was in a four-storey building; we stayed in the shelters all the time and we only ventured upstairs to get some provisions - I didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But whoever wanted to go to Zuc through the town, they had to pass through your neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Well, our neighbourhood was crossed by the main street, but there were other streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mean in that same quarter of town?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the immediate proximity of your house, some 100 metres away, there was the TV building, was there not?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes. Some 100, 150 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. And nearby there was the power transformer station, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was also the Novi Grad municipality building nearby, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes, behind the TV building. There was only one street separating the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The wire factory was close by as well, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what it was that they manufactured?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know because I was further back.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will not be asking you to speak of the details of the incident. This is part of the case file. At any rate you don't know where the shell that hit came from. You, yourself, don't know but you only heard stories about it. Can you please confirm that?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And finally, let me ask you about something else that concerns your second statement. That's Exhibit 115, paragraph 2. There, you describe the arrival of CNN journalists. Upon your return from the hospital, CNN journalists came to visit you at home, and they talked to you and they filmed you, I guess.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You had heard from a relative of yours that he had seen footage of you on the TV.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you recall whether you told the journalists about where the shell had come from?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Well, they were quite a few people there, and all of them talked. There was a whole group of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You talked about what the stories were about where the shell had come from.

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you don't recall whether the footage that was made talked about where the shell had come from?

utterances.speaker: ANDJA GOTOVAC
utterances.text: I don't know. I only cared about getting out of the hospital and going home. I didn't care about stories at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Gotovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have completed my cross-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Just for my own edification, Mr. Lukic, you referred here at page 44, line 18, to Exhibit 115. Exhibit 115, are you talking about exhibits in this case?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that I made a note correctly. I believe that the second statement is Exhibit 115, unless I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I tried to memorise the numbers, but I made a mistake. So I meant the second statement, which is now Exhibit 125.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination, Mr. Cannata?

utterances.speaker: MR. CANNATA
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge? Judge? Ma'am, thank you so much for coming to testify in the Tribunal. This brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. You are now released. You may stand down. Please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, the next scheduled witness, Mr. Gicevic, is nearly ready to begin his testimony, and there is a short proofing note which has just -- literally just been e-mailed to the Defence. Of course, they will need a few minutes to look at that. What I might recommend, if it's appropriate with the Trial Chamber, is perhaps we could break in a few moments and resume perhaps at noon, as if we would take the third session beginning at 12.00, and then the witness should be ready to go, and we should complete that witness today, and I believe the Defence will be ready to cross-examine as well, if that would be appropriate with the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we break, I'm wondering whether, because we have a few moments, whether the Prosecution might be allowed to provide a short oral reply to a response that my colleagues submitted last week related to a pending Prosecution motion related to the testimony of General Wilson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe we're referring to the issue of unscheduled incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. I'm in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Chamber would like to know how you place yourself in its hands. Do you have any objections to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't believe that I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I don't -- based upon the nature of the give and take of motion work, I don't believe that I will be responding, unless the Chamber wants me specifically to respond to whatever. I think that's kind of the end of the give and take as between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: But if you wish to give me another opportunity, I can probably bumble through.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not unless you ask for it, and it's duly considered.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Saxon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Simply two points in reply, Your Honour, to the response that my learned colleagues submitted last week. First of all, the Defence argue that if the Prosecution is permitted to lead this evidence of this particular incident of massive shelling in Sarajevo on the 14th of May, 1992, the Defence will be prejudiced because, according to the Defence, the Defence has not received this information or this notice that this evidence would be led in a timely fashion. On the contrary, about a year and a half ago, I believe it was in February of 2007, Your Honours, in the -- when the Prosecution filed its Rule 65 summaries, the summary for Mr. Wilson included the following information: "He will describe the shelling of Sarajevo and in particular a bombardment on the order of 5 to 10.000 rounds of artillery that occurred on 14 May 1992." Then later on: "He will testify about notice received by the FRY authorities from him directly and from other international representatives about the shelling of civilian targets in Sarajevo." So certainly this particular event was something that the Defence was on notice of.
