Lastly, the Defence have argued that this evidence will not serve to help prove -- to demonstrate the notice that was available to Mr. Perisic about the events that were occurring in Sarajevo at that time in 1992. First of all, Mr. Wilson will testify, and this is in his prior transcript, that his United Nations team had to redeploy to Belgrade following this period of shelling, which, in the Prosecution's submission, provides -- would provide very strong notice to the authorities in Belgrade of events happening in Sarajevo. And second of all, Mr. Wilson will be able to testify that his colleagues informed him about the attention that this event received in the news media in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Those are my only points in reply, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a concern about this motion, Mr. Saxon, which I would like to raise with you, if you can help us. There was a Rule 73 bis decision by the Pre-Trial Chamber, I think it was in 2006 or 1997, I can't remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 15 May 2007, which clearly told the Prosecution how to go about filing these reports, and it indicated that the Prosecution must give four weeks' notice -- wait a minute. It indicated by when these reports were supposed to be filed, isn't it so?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't have a copy of it before me, so I'm trying to talk from memory, if I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it doesn't seem as if they were filed during the stipulated period of time, were they?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct. If I may, though, by way of explanation, it is simply --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me establish the facts before you explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's stipulated by when these filings shall be made. This filing comes well over a year after that stipulation. It comes without any explanation why it comes so late. There is no good cause shown why it should be -- it should be coming at this stage. There's no prior for -- condemnation for the late filing. I find -- and furthermore, the filing, if that order, I remember it well, says that whatever filing must come, must come on four weeks' notice. This filing comes less than four weeks -- less than four weeks' notice, again without any explanation. I am left with the impression that it doesn't seem as if the orders of the Trial Chamber or the Pre-Trial Chamber mean anything to the Prosecution. Am I wrong in this impression?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: With great respect, I believe that you are wrong, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to these motions, for example, with respect to Mr. Wilson, the Prosecution filed this motion as soon as it was clear that Mr. Wilson was going to be available to testify this week. It has simply been extremely difficult for the Prosecution to schedule its witnesses four weeks in advance and to, if I may speak in the vernacular, to nail down its witness schedule that far in advance. So as soon as the Prosecution was sure that these witnesses would be coming - Mr. Wilson and also Mr. Bell - then the Prosecution filed its motion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You haven't demonstrated where I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me -- I said to you, even in your filing of your notice to call these witnesses, you're not addressing the issues -- you're not addressing your violations of the order of 2007. Now, I understand that you may not be able to nail your witnesses -- the scheduling of your witnesses in a way that you would like to, but at least I would like you to give us that kind of explanation in your motion when you ask to call the witness, not to give it orally now when the Bench is asking you. And therefore I still ask my question: I get the impression that the rulings of the Trial Chamber and the Pre-Trial Chamber don't seem to mean much to the Prosecution, and am I wrong in that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, again with great respect, I believe that position is not correct. If the Prosecution has done anything to suggest otherwise, then I apologise on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But are you saying, am I wrong in suggesting that not only did you not comply with the ruling of May 2007, but you also do not give any explanation why you failed to comply and ask for leave then to be allowed to act and your action be regarded as if it was -- it was in compliance with that order. Did you do so in your motion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You didn't. Am I wrong, then, in my impression?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Again, with great respect, Your Honour, if -- obviously that was an oversight. But the very fact that the Prosecution filed these motions as soon as it could is actually, Your Honour, it's an indication that we are doing our best to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether we're talking at cross-purposes. I understand that. All I'm saying is, as you did file those motions, you were aware of the decision of the Pre-Trial Chamber of May 2007, and you were aware that your actions were in violation of those, but you don't seem to say in your motion, I'm aware that I've been ordered this way; I've not been able to comply and I ask you to please condone my failure for the following reasons. You're not saying so in your motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'll ask you a fourth time for you to accept. That's my concern, you see. I just find that the Prosecution doesn't seem to pay any attention to the rulings of the Trial Chamber, or even the Pre-Trial Chamber, and thinks that -- and, besides that ruling, you actually have another remedy under Rule 73 bis (F) which you could have brought in and given good cause why you want to expand on your list, notwithstanding the ruling of May 2007. You didn't adopt that route either. Having said that, I've heard your arguments. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said we'll come back at 12?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: At 12, Your Honour, if that would be all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The thing is -- okay. We'll work it out. We'll take a break and come back at 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I suggest that now that we're starting at 12 instead of 12.30, we go up to half past 1.00 and break for the day. So we'll go for one and a half hours this time instead of 1 hour, 15 minutes. Is that okay? Thank you. Yes, Mr. Saxon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Ms. April Carter will lead the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: May it please the Court, the office of the Prosecution calls Alen Gicevic. Mr. Gicevic is a 92 ter witness, and he also has given evidence in the Dragomir Milosevic case in respect of scheduled incident B11, occurring on 3 March 1995. Witness Gicevic, among others, was shot while riding on a tram in Sarajevo. The witness testified that the shots came from the direction of Grbavica, a Bosnian Serb-held position, and that there were no military targets where the witness was shot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. While you're on your feet, Madam Carter, Mr. Gicevic is not a protected witness, does not have any protective measures at all?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, sir. You may be seated. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Gicevic, you arrived at the Tribunal just this morning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: However, this morning we did have the opportunity to meet, and we went over your previous testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honours, the transcript bears the 65 ter number of 9288.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Mr. Gicevic, you had the opportunity to read through that transcript with a translator by the name of Ivana Manic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And in going through that transcript, there were a few clarifications that needed to be made; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Specifically, there was a concern at page 1556, at lines 3 and 4, that it had indicated that the tram that you were travelling on was going from east to west, and you clarified later in the transcript, at 1556, lines 23 and 24, and again today, that, in fact, that tram was travelling the directions of west to east. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: It's correct. The tram went from the west to the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: There was also a concern at transcript page 1564, lines 6 to 9, in regards to the containers that were placed at certain intersections in Sarajevo. When you indicate that the containers were three to four deep, you're referring to containers being stacked upon each other, three to four high; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And lastly, at transcript page 1565, line 6, there's a term used, "Salvation Route." Now, you have indicated that this is not a term that you had used, and you had used solely "Route of Life," which comes just before it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I said it was the "Road of Life." It's a minor difference, for those who know the terminology.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: So you're indicating the term is "Road" as opposed to "Route of Life." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: After these clarifications have been made, do you accept that if you were asked those same questions today, that your answers would be the same?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would seek at this time admittance of 65 ter number 9288.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 9288 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P128, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. While we're there, Madam Carter, the Chamber hasn't been provided with the 65 ter copies. Is there any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: One moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the 65 ter exhibits were released into e-court, but you're correct, we did not provide a hard copy of those documents. I do have a hard copy of the transcript, for the ease of the Court, that I can certainly provide, but I would have to seek a break in order to provide hard copies of the remainder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We would rather not break, Madam Carter. Proceed. But at a convenient time, if you can provide us with the copies, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour, they will be provided momentarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, when you went over the transcript, there were also seven exhibits that were admitted within the transcript that we had gone through as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And specifically, those exhibits are 65 ter number 9282, which was Prosecution Exhibit 163 in the Milosevic case, which was your witness statement of 15 November 1995; 65 ter number 9283, previously admitted as P164 in the Milosevic case, your witness statement of 21 April 2006; 65 ter number 9284, exhibited as P165 in Milosevic, which is a map marked by you; 65 ter 9285, previously Exhibit P166 in the Milosevic case, an additional map marked by you; 65 ter number 9286, previously P167, a map marked by you; 65 ter 9287, previously Exhibit P168, a map marked by you; and finally, 65 ter exhibit 4380, which in the Milosevic case was D23 but has been exhibited in this case as P36, which is the criminal investigation file for the incident of 3 March 1995. Are you adopting these exhibits as well?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time the Prosecution seeks to tender 65 ter numbers 9282 through 9287, and seek admittance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. 65 ter 9282 through 9287 are admitted into evidence. May they please be given exhibit numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter 09282 will be Exhibit P129, Your Honours; 65 ter 09283 will be Exhibit P130; 65 ter 09284 will be Exhibit P131; 65 ter 09285 will be Exhibit P132; 65 ter 09286 will be Exhibit P133; and 65 ter 09287 will be Exhibit P134, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, madam. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: As your previous transcript was quite complete, I want to cover only two topics with you here today. The first, I want to discuss with you the location of the sniping incident, and the last thing I want to discuss with you is the route -- excuse me, the "Road of Life."

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If I can bring up 65 ter number 8598, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, in your previous testimony, you did get the opportunity to mark certain locations within Sarajevo relevant to the sniping; however, this is a picture that is far more detailed, as it's giving a much tighter picture of the site of the sniping incident. So if you can please mark on this exhibit where specifically the sniping incident occurred, if you can circle it and then mark it with a 1.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In your previous testimony at page 1570, the Defence counsel in that case had tried to identify certain positions that may have been military in nature, and you spoke of a number of these buildings surrounding the site of the sniping incident and were explaining their civilian function, so I'd like to have this exhibit marked with some of those buildings. First, can you identify with a number 2 the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you put an X over it, so you're indicating that the yellow building to the top middle of the screen is the Holiday Inn, and you're marking it number 2; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's the Holiday Inn hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you now identify and mark the philosophy building with a 3.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Can you identify and mark the museum with a 4.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of any of these buildings, the Holiday Inn, the philosophy building, or the museum, being used in any sort of military function?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no military installations there.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Where was the closest military installation to the site of your sniping incident?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Within the compound of the Marsal Tito barracks, and that is this vacant area where buildings had been earlier. That's where the UNPROFOR was based. And a bit to the left, to the west, was the traffic police building. You cannot see it in this picture because it's further to the left, after the picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: And I see that you've marked the Marsal Tito barracks with an X and a 5 denoting that distance. Can you tell me, in metres, how far away were the barracks from where you were shot?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: That could be approximately 400, 500 metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to have this exhibit marked into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 8598 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Sir, you also had spoken of this "Road of Life," and that was at transcript 156423. In order to explain a little bit further to the Court, I'm going to have 65 ter number 8600 brought up. But in the interim, can you please explain to the Court what was the "Road of Life," and what was the significance to the people of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: The "Road of Life" was the road used by people for their own traffic, for transport, and it was safer than any other communication. It was safer than anything else, but it was not absolutely safe because it was also the target of sniping. Outside that road, in front of the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska, there was a large number of buildings which provided cover for the people and the vehicles that used the road. All the other roads were much less safe and much closer to the separation lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: When we spoke earlier, you had indicated that this was one of the only roads in Sarajevo that could be travelled by foot; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but even that did not have absolute protection, because at intersections and crossroads, you couldn't cover all the points to guarantee safety for the traffic of people and vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Okay. How was food and water brought in for the people of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think this is going out of the scope of 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ms. Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the question is about the "Road of Life." I'm just trying to get for the Court a clearer picture about the import of this route to both this witness as well as to the people of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then ask about the "Road of Life," Madam Carter, not about food and water.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Outside of the people commuting along this road, was this road used for any other purpose?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Since it was the only relatively safe road, it was used for all possible purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Can you name purposes, other than the commuting of the people, that this road was used for.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the traffic of people and goods, to the extent that it was possible to transport things from the west to the east at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Now, 65 ter 8600 is now before you, and I would ask you to mark along this photograph in blue the route of life -- excuse me, the "Road of Life."

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: This is just the shortest section of this so-called "Road of Life," which ran for another 7 or 8 kilometres to the west.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: In addition to the "Road of Life," I would like you to mark in red, if possible, the front line in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: This is approximately up to the bridge on Vrbanja river and to the left of the Jewish cemetery and on to the east.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I would like to seek to admit this exhibit into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 8600 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number. Sorry, the marked 8600 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: At this time, Your Honour, the Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, ma'am. Sorry, let me just find something out. You said P135, Madam Registrar, not 136?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 135, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what was 65 ter 8958? What exhibit is that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour is correct. It would be -- 8958 would be 135, and P100 marked by the witness will be Exhibit P136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I see your learned friend still on her feet. I thought she had said she had finished her examination, but yes, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: I did, Your Honour. I just wanted for clarification of the record, the 65 ter 8598 that's been annotated by this witness is what I was seeking as Exhibit 135.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. 65 ter 8598 as annotated would be P135. Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Gicevic. My name is Novak Lukic, and on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Perisic, I will question you briefly. I know you arrived recently and went straight to your proofing session, so you must be tired. I understood when I read your previous testimony you were going from Cengic Vila towards Bascarsija, and looking at the picture it's from left to right; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And as you were standing in the tram, Marindvor was to your left, and the Jewish cemetery and Vraca was on your right side.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please wait for a second after my question so we don't overlap. There is interpretation involved. A moment ago you drew a red line to mark the separation line. In fact, it's the Miljacka river. The Miljacka river was the separation line between the territory controlled by the BH army and the territory controlled by the VRS in this photograph; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we agree that from Miljacka river, from that separation line, to the Zmaja Od Bosna Street where the tram was running, there is 200 or 300 metres, roughly.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Roughly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gicevic, you did not see where the bullet that hit you came from.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But you supposed, and that's transcript page 1557 from the Dragomir Milosevic case, what the location could be, so you drew one location, one highrise building, 12 to 13 floors, and the other possible location is the Metalka company building.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I designated those two as possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And you designated them, as you said in your first statement given to the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY, on page 1559, you said the same thing, you designated them that way because you said those were the locations of the most notorious Serbs.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't say anything about the most notorious Serbs. I said that sniper bullets could have come from that side. I never used the word "notorious" in reference to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your first statement to the OTP, 15 November 1995, we don't have the same numbering of paragraphs but I believe it's the ninth sentence where you say, quote: "The Chetniks held those positions. When I say 'Chetniks,' I mean the worst part of the Serb population."

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: And it is completely different to what you said before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You are right. So to the best of your knowledge, those positions were held by people to whom you referred as Chetniks and to whom you referred as the most notorious part of the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Judge Robinson asked you - that's at page 1559, line 10 - if you had a specific reason to believe that the shots were fired from that location and you said that you could only assume that the shots came from those buildings because they were easily to be seen from the tram; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: A moment ago you indicated on the map certain buildings that Madam Prosecutor asked you about, and you indicated the location of the museum building and of the faculty of philosophy building, I believe. You said that, to your knowledge, the BH army did not have its positions there.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, no, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At any rate the buildings were situated in the territory under the control of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To your right, that's to say, that particular area was to your right in relation to the direction in which you were moving.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Reading the transcripts from your earlier testimony, I realised that earlier on, some ten months before the incident, you were a member of the army. You were there as a nurse.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I was a medical corps driver and, when necessary, also as a nurse, and in July 1994 I was demobilised.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Therefore, you cannot claim with any certainty where the BH army positions were at the time when you were wounded.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I could not, but between the building and the tram that was in motion, there were UNPROFOR APCs, and, in fact, the bullets would have to pass through these APCs before hitting the passengers in the tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And were these positions also along the route of the tram?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On all the intersections that I marked on the map there were UNPROFOR APCs to be seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let me just clarify my question. When the Prosecutor asked you at page 59, line 1, in English, the question was as follows: In relation to the museum, the holiday inn building and the faculty of philosophy building, whether there were facilities that had a military function. And you answered, as it was entered in the English language, there were no buildings that were military instillations. That's how it was entered in the English version. To make it clear, in your view, you believed that there were no members of the BH army positioned along those facilities. That's your opinion, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From the position where you stood in the tram, and you were moving in such a way that you were facing the right bank of the Miljacka, could you see both of the buildings of the museum and the faculty of philosophy from your vantage point?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will put a couple of questions to you in order to clarify the details concerning the shot or the shots. All this time you have been claiming, to put it that way, that there were several shots, that you heard two to three shots.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I kept saying that it seemed to me that I heard two or three shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps I'm being too specific in my question, but I'd like to know the following: Do you remember whether, in addition to these two to three shots, any sounds of the pane smashing and so on?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps there were two shots and then the third sound was that of the window-pane smashing, or perhaps it was a different ratio. But it's very difficult to clearly distinguish all these sounds when one is being shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time you were in the company of your girlfriend.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, who is my wife today.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not wish to inquire in such great detail. You went to the hospital with her, did you not?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss the number of shots fired later on with her? Did you ask her how many shots she had heard?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, she is listening to our discussion right now, and she also believed that there were two to three shots fired. Women, by nature, are more fearful so I guess she managed to gather less of the reality than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In addition to the documents, the criminal file of the case was also entered into evidence, which includes, among other things, the statement of Asima Bacvic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Bacvic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Asima Bacvic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is to be found, that is to say, the criminal file, under number 35. I don't know if we can see that in e-court. In the B/C/S, 00331681 is the number. P36.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is it P36 or P35, sir? What are you asking for? You said 36 or 35?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. P36 is the criminal file related to the incident of the 3rd of March, 1995. The page in the B/C/S that I have is 03316381, although I do know that the court officer doesn't find the ERN numbers helpful. I think it's page -- either 23 or 24 of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just interject while we're looking for the page. Could you please also remember to pause a little bit after the witness has answered so that you don't overlap, and could you also do the same, sir, pause after the question has been put to you so that you don't overlap and give the interpreters an opportunity to interpret. Yes, Madam Carter.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: If it would be of assistance to the Court, Your Honour, the English page that is being spoken of, there are multiple translations within P36. The translation being spoken of right now is 0331-6361-1, at page 23.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is page 1 of the document, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gicevic, I will read this out to you, a portion of the statement given by your wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the English version, and can we now have the Serbian version as well so that Mr. Gicevic can have the benefit of it. Thank you. No, that's not the one. That one belongs to another person. A page earlier, please. Two pages ahead of that one in the Serbian version. There it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you see it somewhere in the middle? "When the vehicle was close to the museum, I heard the bullet hit the tram and all the passengers hauled themselves onto the ground." Based on this statement, I see that this is her statement, and I know from the previous trial that the driver had also said that he had heard one bullet only. Is it possible that you made a mistake?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: It is possible, but I do stand by what I said earlier, that there were two to three shots or hits.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While we have the statement on the screen, let me indicate that I noticed another issue that is different in your wife's statement from what you said. You said that you left the tram and went to the hospital on foot. First you said that you took a taxi, and then you corrected yourself and said that you went there on foot.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I looked at the statement this morning, and it was quite illogical for me to proceed from the taxi rank, which was close to Zagreb Hospital, to take a taxi and cross the distance which was only of some 100 metres. It was a very short distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you stand by what you said?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that we took Albanska Street from Zagreb Hotel, or rather from the tram stop, and reached the hospital on foot.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So you believe that she made a mistake there?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't think that she herself claims that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Well, look at it. Down there at he bottom it says: " ... at the taxi rank close to the Zagreb Hotel, a taxi driver got us in a car and took us to the state hospital where she was treated," and so on and so forth, "where Alen was treated," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I can tell you what my case is. I doubt, on the basis of the other statements, that there were more shots. I believe that there was one shot which hurt somebody in the tram. In that sense, let me remind you that when -- at page 1580, Judge Robinson asked you if you remembered how that other individual was seated, the one that you noticed was also injured in the tram, you said literally, page 15 -- line 58, you said that your recollection of it was hazy or vague. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was probably the case. If you asked me where various individuals were seated in the tram that I rode on yesterday, I would probably have difficulty in recalling it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can it be, then, that your recollection concerning the number of shots fired was also hazy? Let me put this hypothesis to you: Since you were injured and you saw another individual being injured, is it possible that on the basis of this you concluded that there were several shots?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Initially, I said that there were one to two shots. Then I said that I wasn't sure whether these were two shots or whether there was also another sound of items smashing, and that's how I ended up saying that there were, I believed, two to three shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You were shot to your left upper leg; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: A bit above the knee.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The bullet stayed in your leg, and it was taken out only a couple of days later.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was no exit wound, but it was only the bullet case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is that what you were told in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: It's not that I was told only. I was given the bullet case, to take it home, and I eventually threw it away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There's one other thing I'd like to know. You said that you were a nurse or an orderly and a driver. Where was it, in the military hospital, at the time that you were mobilised?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not work in the military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How did you come to know that the media representatives were always in the military hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: Because my sister and my father-in-law worked in the military hospital. I know that always at the Kosevo Military Hospital or, rather, outside of the hospital, there were international news crews, journalists, waiting to take statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you in a position to follow the news over the media in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: During the rare moments when we had electricity, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you informed of the shelling and sniping of the Grbavica area by the BH army from the media? Did you ever hear anything of the sort from the media?

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not have occasion to. We only listened to the local media.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that the local media did not want to report on possible actions taken against civilians on the other side.

utterances.speaker: ALEN GICEVIC
utterances.text: It's quite possible, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have completed my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Lukic. Madam Carter, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Judge? Judge? Mr. Gicevic, this brings us to the end of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to testify. You are now excused. You may go home. You may stand down. And please travel well back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Carter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAXON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, that concludes the Prosecution's witnesses for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Saxon. Do you want to be excused, Madam Carter?

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are excused. Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber is now going to give -- may the Chamber please move into private session. 15 [Private session] [Confidentiality lifted by later order of the Chamber]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. This is now an oral order concerning the motions by the Prosecution with respect to Mr. Martin Bell and Mr. John Wilson. On the 10th of October, 2008, and on the 13th of October, 2008, the Prosecution filed respectively a motion for leave to lead evidence of unscheduled incidents from Witness Martin Bell, with annexes, and a motion for leave to lead evidence of unscheduled incidents from Witness Brigadier General John Wilson. The Defence filed its two responses to the motions on the 21st of October, 2008. The Prosecution motions were filed pursuant to the Rule 73 bis decision of 15th May 2007, which requires the Prosecution to apply for leave of the Trial Chamber to lead evidence of unscheduled incidents upon a showing that such evidence is essential to prove an important aspect of the case at least four weeks prior to the scheduled testimony. The Trial Chamber recalls that this time limit was not respected by the Prosecution. The Trial Chamber notes that the Defence has agreed not to raise objection on this ground for these two instances; however, the Trial Chamber further notes that this fact does not prevent the Trial Chamber from dismissing the motions on this ground. Both motions were filed less than three weeks prior to the scheduled testimony. This is in direct violation of paragraph 17 of Rule 73 bis decision of 15th May 2007, wherein the Pre-Trial Chamber ordered that "the Prosecution must file a motion requesting the leave of the Trial Chamber to lead such evidence at least four weeks in advance of the scheduled testimony." The Trial Chamber notes the Prosecution's arguments in its oral reply of today regarding the difficulties faced in scheduling the witness order. The Trial Chamber, however, finds that scheduling difficulties are irrelevant when it comes to compliance with an order of the Pre-Trial or Trial Chamber. It would have been appropriate for the Prosecution to at least file a notice that it intended to lead evidence of unscheduled incidents on four weeks -- four weeks in advance, considering that in the Prosecution's own admission, it was aware of the scope of these witness testimonies since at least February 2007, when the 65 ter summaries were filed. The Trial Chamber notes the Prosecution has not provided any good cause or, in fact, any explanation at all for this violation of the Pre-Trial Chamber's order. The Trial Chamber therefore denies the Prosecution motion to lead the proposed evidence of Mr. Bell and Mr. Wilson on unscheduled incidents. That concludes the oral decision. Are there any housekeeping matters that any of the parties would like to raise before we take an adjournment? Mr. Saxon? Mr. Lukic? My schedule of the trial still says that we are going into Courtroom III tomorrow. Does anybody have an updated schedule that says we are coming to Courtroom II?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
